newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: End of sanctions for Yugoslavia waits for U.S..
newsitem.headline: End of sanctions for Yugoslavia waits for U.S..

text.p: Russia and the United States were unable on to agree on when to end sanctions against Yugoslavia, thereby postponing a Security Council resolution on the subject, diplomats said.
Russia's ambassador Sergei Lavrov had drawn up a document that would end the sanctions on Tuesday but the United States rejected it, saying the elections had not been certified yet.
The sanctions were suspended by the council last November as a follow up to the U.S.-initiated Balkan peace accords signed in Dayton, Ohio last year.
The council's resolution stipulated the sanctions would be lifted entirely 10 days after the Bosnian elections, which to Moscow meant Tuesday, Sept. 24.

But the United States has interpreted the resolution as saying the 10-day countdown should begin after the the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), certified the elections were fair.
"The OSCE must certify that the elections met the standards set up by the Dayton accords," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns in New York on Monday.
"The United States is very clear that the 10-day period refers to the period after certification by the OSCE and that has not happened yet," he said.
Burns said Secretary of State Warren Christopher had discussed the issue with his Russian counterpart, Yevgeny Primakov on Monday, with Lavrov present. It was not known if they reached any agreement.
At the same time the six-nation "contact group" that determines Balkan policy in the Security Council met at the United Nations without completing a draft resolution.

Also at issue is whether the lifting of sanctions includes allowing Yugoslavia to rejoin the U.N. General Assembly and the U.N. Economic and Social Council as well as other international bodies where its membership has been suspended.
Diplomats said Washington had problems with a proposal by Russia that Yugoslavia be allowed to join the General Assembly and other U.N. bodies.

The United States has said previously it would keep a so-called outer ring of sanctions, such as preventing the rump Yugoslav state of Serbia and Montenegro from institutions like the International Monetary Fund. Washington can block Belgrade's participation in some of these institutions unilaterally.

In addition the United States was considering inserting into the resolution a possible reimposition of sanctions should any of the Bosnian parties not comply with the election results in an effort to keep some leverage on Yugoslavia, which in turn could pressure the Bosnian Serbs.

Momcilo Krajisnik, the Bosnian Serb representative in the newly-elected Bosnian presidency and an outspoken advocate of Serb secession, has refused to travel to Sarajevo for an initial meeting of the three-member state presidency.
This new body would be chaired by Moslem President Alija Izetbegovic who won the most votes and include Kremiri Zuban, the Croat representative,
The contact group members, in addition to the United States and Russia, are Britain, France, Germany and Italy.
